title: How design shapes space choice behaviors in public urban and shared indoor spaces- A review
review_question: This study investigates the benefits and drawbacks of common indoor and public outdoor spaces, compares trade-offs between open and enclosed spaces, and identifies analogous synergies and insights applicable across urban planning and building design scales. Specifically, it addresses: 1. Distribution of research topics in space allocation; 2. Distribution of methods used; 3. Main drivers for research; 4. Physical and socio-physical influences on space choice behaviors; 5. Benefits and drawbacks for shared/public space implementation; 6. Trade-offs between open and enclosed environments and their balance.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Initial search terms supplemented by keywords from landmark papers. Three iterative Google Scholar searches (2015-2019 inclusive). Excluded tangential research fields (energy, agriculture, robotics). Filtered by document types and titles for contextual relevance. Abstracts screened for relevance to research questions. Quality appraisal based on method definition, conclusion validity, and impact.

synthesis_conclusions: Public urban spaces and common building spaces share characteristics as physical links and multi-purpose spaces, but there is a lack of sufficient spaces for retreat and concentration.
The shift towards collaborative and flexible work approaches increases the need for quiet informal spaces in future workplaces and learning environments.
Flexibility in space design supports both interaction/collaboration and individual activities requiring high focus.
Optimal space conditions require integrating multiple spatial qualities to balance opposing concepts and promote diverse activities.
Mutual barriers for common spaces (economic prioritization, policy, equipment, densification, environmental comfort, accessibility) are analogous between building and urban scales.
Layout, design quality, ambient environmental conditions, and support structures are main determinants of spatial choices.
Atmosphere and character are more important for optional activities, while furnishing is more important for work activities.
Common spaces are not universally suitable for all activities and depend on additional support functions.
Spaciousness and technology/communication infrastructure are common functional barriers for work.
Locational accessibility and functionality are crucial to counteract negative effects of common/public spaces.
Aesthetic appearance relates to satisfaction but less to occupancy preferences.
Perception, cognition, and behavior are key to assessing human responses to the built environment.
Common spaces should support psychological aspects, self-efficacy, social relationships, and functional support for basic activities.
Crowdedness, territoriality, privacy, interaction, self-control, and autonomy are key socio-physical determinants, often contrasting open vs. enclosed spaces.
Successful common spaces can increase interaction, demographic diversity, and democratic processes.
Flexibility and adjustability positively influence user attitudes, motivation, engagement, and well-being.
Crowdedness and noise levels are critical for space perception and satisfaction.
evidence_gaps: Lack of sophisticated findings about scalable benefits of different space typologies due to limited flexibility of SLRs.
Unilateral research methods, with surveys and literature reviews dominating, leading to issues of context-dependency and lack of scalability.
Poor representation of studies using digital data collection means (sensors, cameras, wearable devices) to investigate human behavior in physical settings.
Lack of funding for digital data collection tools, routines in research procedures, and time limitations hinder methodological diversity.
Opportunity for urban studies to emphasize social spaces and space choices more.
Opportunity for building studies to emphasize green spaces and the built environment more.
Opportunity for building studies to focus more on well-being and lifestyles.
Direct differentiation of health and well-being effects in open and enclosed spaces is rarely targeted.
risk_of_bias_assessment: Quality appraisal was conducted using criteria: method explicitly defined and sound, conclusions follow data, results meaningful/applicable, overall recommendation for inclusion. No formal risk of bias tool (e.g., PRISMA) was specified.
limitations: Structured literature reviews have limitations in creativity and intuition when searching for literature, not allowing high flexibility in tailoring search directions.
SLRs highly depend on the quality of titles and abstracts of search findings.
Limited flexibility of SLRs results in a lack of sophisticated findings about scalable benefits of different space typologies.
Methods used are rather unilateral (surveys, literature reviews), leading to context-dependency and lack of scalability.
Digital data collection methods (sensors, cameras, wearable devices) are poorly represented.
Lack of funding, routines, and time limitations contribute to the lack of methodological diversity.
